1177.title: The banyan in the seed
1177.hook: Uddalaka has his son break open a banyan seed, and Samkhya argues the effect is already in its cause
1177.carry: the effect already lives in its cause
1177.tomorrow: Why would the seer and the world ever meet?
1177.howItsDone: Students of Indian philosophy learn the debate over causation, Samkhya's view that the effect pre-exists in its cause against the Nyaya-Vaisheshika view that it is newly made, and the Chandogya's banyan seed is told in homes and classrooms as a picture of the unseen essence.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the Samkhya Karika reasoned its way to the witness: a bed is made for a sleeper outside it. Today, the Karika on cause and effect, and a much older story about a seed.
screen: `A BED FOR SOMEONE.` · `A SEED, BROKEN OPEN.`

segments.voice: In the Chandogya Upanishad, a young man named Shvetaketu comes home after twelve years of study, quite pleased with himself. His father, Uddalaka, asks him one question his teachers never covered, and the son can't answer it. So the father teaches him at home. Bring me a fruit from that banyan tree, he says. Break it. What do you see? Tiny seeds, sir. Break one of those. What do you see now? Nothing at all, sir.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS OF STUDY.` → `BREAK THE SEED.` → `NOTHING AT ALL, SIR.`

segments.voice: And the father says, in paraphrase: that fine essence you can't see, my son, is what this whole great banyan stands on. The tree was already in the seed. Earlier in the same lesson he asks a sharper question: how could something that is come from what is not? Centuries later the Samkhya Karika turned that kind of intuition into an argument, and named it in one verse: sat karyam, the effect already is. That's satkarya. Its reasons: nothing comes from what doesn't exist at all; you need the right material; not everything comes from everything. Commentators give an example still used in classrooms: press sesame and you get oil, press sand all day and you get none. The old teachers also point to milk becoming curd, and Nani's kitchen still shows it: a spoon of yesterday's curd in warm milk, one quiet night, and by morning, dahi. Nobody built it. It unfolded. So for Samkhya, creation isn't something out of nothing. The whole world was folded inside prakriti, the root, and it unfolds. Not every Hindu school agrees. Nyaya and Vaisheshika argue a pot is a genuinely new thing, and the tradition keeps both arguments in the room. Uddalaka takes the seed somewhere Samkhya won't follow: that fine essence, he says, is the self of the whole world, and you are that. Many teachers draw one lesson from both: what you will become isn't bolted on from outside. It's already in you, waiting for its conditions.
screen: `THE TREE WAS IN THE SEED.` · `SAT KARYAM: THE EFFECT ALREADY IS.` · `SESAME GIVES OIL. SAND DOESN'T.` · `NYAYA SAYS: THE POT IS NEW.` · `YOU ARE THAT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and picture the banyan seed, broken open, nothing to see inside. Bring to mind one beginning in your life right now, a friendship, a habit, a hope, and look at it the way Uddalaka looked at the seed: the whole tree already folded in. With each out-breath, let it rest there. If you pray, you can hold that beginning in prayer.
The Samkhya Karika. Its argument on causes: the effect already exists in its cause, so the world unfolds from prakriti instead of appearing from nothing.
screen: `THE SAMKHYA KARIKA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the effect already lives in its cause. The banyan was in the seed. See you tomorrow.

1178.title: Two travelers in the forest
1178.hook: two travelers left behind in a forest, one who can't walk and one who can't see
1178.tomorrow: Why does the dancer leave the stage?
1178.howItsDone: Teachers of Samkhya and of Yoga philosophy explain the meeting of purusha and prakriti with the story of the lame man and the blind man, drawn from the Karika's phrase and its commentaries.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the effect already lives in its cause, the banyan in the seed and the world folded in prakriti. Today, why it unfolds at all.
screen: `THE BANYAN IN THE SEED.` · `TWO TRAVELERS.`

segments.voice: A caravan has been scattered in a forest, and two travelers are left behind. One can't walk. The other can't see. Night is coming. The one who can't walk can see the path, the river, the way out, but he can't take a step. The one who can't see has strong legs and a strong back, but he has no idea which way to go. Alone, both of them stay in the forest. The classic commentaries on the Samkhya Karika tell this little story, and the Karika itself names it in a single phrase. Today it explains how the whole world got moving.
screen: `A CARAVAN SCATTERED.` → `ONE CAN'T WALK, ONE CAN'T SEE.` → `ALONE, BOTH STAY LOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the ending. The traveler who can't see lifts the other onto his shoulders. Now one does the walking and the other does the seeing, and together they get out of the forest. Once they reach the village, they go their separate ways. The Karika uses this picture for the two from Samkhya's opening days. Prakriti is the one with legs: she moves, changes and unfolds, but she has no seeing of her own. Purusha is the one with eyes: the witness, who sees but never acts. Their coming together, the verse says, is like the lame and the blind, and creation unfolds from that meeting. And the Karika says what the meeting is for. It's so that purusha can see prakriti, and so that purusha can finally be set free. In Samkhya the world isn't an accident, and it isn't a trap someone built. Here is the teaching, plainly: in Samkhya the world exists for the self, first for experience, then for freedom. Notice too how the story ends. The two travelers part ways. That's where Samkhya is heading. Not everyone in the Hindu tradition tells the end of the journey this way. Vedanta, at the close of this season, has its own account. A partnership that neither side could manage alone, that gets somewhere, and then lets go.
screen: `ONE CARRIES, ONE GUIDES.` · `PRAKRITI MOVES, PURUSHA SEES.` · `A MEETING WITH A PURPOSE.` · `THE TRAVELERS PART WAYS.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand on your knee, lift it a little and lower it again, a few times: the hand is the one with legs, and it moves. Then notice the seeing, aware of the movement without lifting anything, and let the hand go still: let the body carry, let the seeing see. If you pray, you can offer thanks for the body that carries you.
The Samkhya Karika. Its picture of the world's beginning: prakriti, who moves but can't see, and purusha, who sees but can't move, getting out of the forest together.
screen: `THE SAMKHYA KARIKA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: prakriti moves, purusha sees. One carries, one guides, and together they get out. That's today, done.

1179.title: The dancer takes her bow
1179.hook: the ankle bells go quiet and the dancer leaves the stage: Samkhya's picture of the world's show
1179.carry: once truly seen, prakriti ends her dance
1179.tomorrow: If no one is bound, who gets free?
1179.howItsDone: The dancer image from the Samkhya Karika is taught in Samkhya and Yoga study as a picture of liberation through discernment.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the Samkhya Karika gave two travelers: prakriti moves, purusha sees, and together they get out of the forest.
screen: `TWO TRAVELERS.` · `THE DANCER.`

segments.voice: The last rhythm of a classical dance recital. The drummer's hands slow. The dancer strikes her final pose, ankle bells ringing, then still. For a moment nobody in the hall moves. Then she bows, and walks off the stage. She doesn't come back out to do it all again for the same people. The dance was for them, it was seen, and it's finished. The Samkhya Karika reaches for exactly this scene near its end, when it tries to say what happens once the world has done what it came to do.
screen: `THE FINAL POSE.` → `SHE BOWS AND WALKS OFF.` → `SEEN, AND FINISHED.`

segments.voice: The verse goes like this, in paraphrase. As a dancer stops dancing once she has shown herself to the audience, so prakriti stops, once she has shown herself to purusha. Hold yesterday's travelers in mind. Prakriti carried the seer through the forest so that purusha could see. The whole unfolding, everything in the count, has been a performance with one audience in view. The Karika adds two more touches. First, prakriti is generous. She serves purusha in many ways, the text says, and asks nothing back. Purusha does nothing in return; it can't. It only watches. Second, prakriti is modest. The Karika says nothing is more modest than she is. Once she knows she has been truly seen, she doesn't show herself to that seer again. And a few verses later the text gives the last exchange, almost like a play. One says, I have seen her, and loses interest. The other says, I have been seen, and stops. That's Samkhya's picture of freedom: liberation by seeing clearly. Later Samkhya and Yoga call that seeing viveka, discernment. And notice what it isn't. It isn't fighting the world, or escaping it, or hating it. It's seeing it so completely that its hold just ends, the way a song you've finally understood stops replaying in your head. The dance isn't wasted. Tomorrow, on the last day of Samkhya: what the seer is left with.
screen: `THE DANCER STOPS WHEN SEEN.` · `PRAKRITI IS GENEROUS.` · `PRAKRITI IS MODEST.` · `I HAVE SEEN HER. I HAVE BEEN SEEN.`

segments.voice: Pick one sound, a breath, a hum in the room, a car going by, and stay with it from its first edge to its last, letting it finish completely. Then wait, quiet, until something else steps onto the stage, and watch that one to its end too. If you pray, you can offer each ending as it comes.
The Samkhya Karika. Its picture of freedom: prakriti as a dancer who, once truly seen, finishes her dance and leaves the stage.

segments.voice: Your line: once truly seen, prakriti ends her dance. The dancer takes her bow. Until tomorrow.

1180.title: The prince raised by hunters
1180.hook: a prince grows up among forest hunters until one sentence tells him who he is
1180.carry: the seer was never really bound
1180.tomorrow: Who was Patanjali, and what is yoga for?
1180.howItsDone: In Samkhya and Yoga study, the closing verses of the Karika on bondage, release and kaivalya are read with commentaries, and teachers use the king's son raised among hunters, and the crystal beside a colored flower, to explain how the witness only seems to be bound.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: once truly seen, prakriti ends her dance, the way a dancer bows and leaves the stage.
screen: `PRAKRITI, TRULY SEEN.` · `THE DANCER BOWS.`

segments.voice: A baby prince is sent away from the palace and grows up in the forest with a tribe of hunters. He hunts with them, eats with them, and thinks of himself as one of them. Why wouldn't he? Years later, a minister of the king finds him and tells him one sentence: you are the king's son. Nothing about the young man changes, not his face, not his hands. And yet he's no longer a hunter. A later Samkhya text, the Samkhya Sutra, sums up the whole story in a few words: like the king's son.
screen: `RAISED BY HUNTERS.` → `YOU ARE THE KING'S SON.` → `NOTHING CHANGES. EVERYTHING DOES.`

segments.voice: That's Samkhya's last surprise, and the Karika says it outright. In paraphrase: no one is really bound, no one is really released, no one really wanders from life to life. It's prakriti, in her many forms, who is bound, wanders and is released. The I-maker, the mind, the feeling of being stuck all sit on prakriti's side. Purusha, the witness, was never in chains, just as the prince was never a hunter. It only seemed so, the way a clear crystal seems red when a red flower sits beside it. So freedom isn't the witness breaking out. It's the mistake clearing up. How? The Karika says by practicing the principles, the count, again and again, until a knowledge arises in three short steps: I am not, nothing is mine, not I. That isn't despair. It means thinking, owning and the sense of me belong to prakriti, and the witness stops claiming them. The goal has a name: kaivalya, aloneness, the seer standing on its own. Many teachers point out that several Hindu schools share this shape, each in its own words: moksha isn't becoming something new. It's recognizing what you always were. Vedanta names that self differently, and this path will get there. Tomorrow, Yoga takes this map and turns it into a practice.
screen: `NO ONE IS REALLY BOUND.` · `THE PRINCE WAS NEVER A HUNTER.` · `I AM NOT, NOTHING IS MINE.` · `KAIVALYA: THE SEER ALONE.`

segments.voice: Let whatever is here come up, a plan, a feeling, a tightness somewhere, and don't argue with it; let it be colored light near the crystal, and notice the crystal itself stays clear. Thoughts can come and go. If you pray, you can pray quietly while the colors pass.
The Samkhya Karika. Its last word on freedom: the witness was never bound. Prakriti is bound and released, and the seer is left alone, kaivalya.

screen: `THE SEER WAS NEVER BOUND.` · `THE KING'S SON.`

segments.voice: This path told this story back in year one. A woman named Gonika stands in a river at dawn, palms cupped full of water to offer to the sun, praying. Far above, the great serpent Adishesha, on whom Vishnu rests, asks to go down and teach. He drops into her open hands as a tiny snake, and becomes a child. She names him for how he came: pata, fallen, into anjali, cupped hands. Patanjali. Pictures still show him with a sage's body and a serpent's coils, a hood of cobra heads above him. Today he returns as the teacher of a whole school.
screen: `PALMS CUPPED AT DAWN.` → `A TINY SERPENT FALLS.` → `PATA, ANJALI: PATANJALI.`

segments.voice: The root text of the Yoga darshana is the Yoga Sutra, credited by tradition to Patanjali. Read it right after the Samkhya Karika and the furniture looks familiar. The seer and the seen. The three gunas. The seen existing for the seer's sake, for experience and for release. That's Samkhya's map, nearly line for line. But the Sutra asks a practical question: how do you get the confusion to clear? Its second verse answers: yoga is the stilling of the movements of the mind. And the next verse says what happens then: the seer rests in its own nature. That's yesterday's crystal, with the red flower moved away. Then Yoga adds two things of its own. First, a whole program of practice: ethics, posture, breath, withdrawing the senses, concentration, meditation, absorption. Second, Ishvara, a special purusha untouched by affliction and karma, and the Sutra offers devotion to Ishvara as one path to stillness. The Samkhya Karika says nothing of Ishvara, and the schools are allowed to differ. It's also why many classes in some lineages, Iyengar's and Ashtanga among them, in India and far beyond it, still begin by chanting an invocation to Patanjali. Yoga isn't stretching with a philosophy attached. It's Samkhya's map, walked, and the teacher gets thanked first.

If you pray, you can rest in Ishvara, or whatever you pray to, as the Sutra allows.
Yoga. As a darshana, the school of Patanjali's Yoga Sutra: Samkhya's map of seer and seen, walked through practice, with room for Ishvara.

1182.title: As hard to hold as the wind
1182.hook: Arjuna tells Krishna the mind is as hard to hold as the wind, and Vyasa maps its five grounds
1182.carry: abhyasa and vairagya hold the restless mind
1182.tomorrow: What did Ratnakara ask his family?
1182.howItsDone: Students of Yoga philosophy read the Yoga Sutras with Vyasa's commentary, often alongside Krishna's answer to Arjuna in the Gita, and teachers use the five grounds of the mind to help a student see where their attention is before they practice.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yoga as a school: yoga stills the mind so the seer rests. Patanjali, fallen into open hands.
screen: `YOGA STILLS THE MIND.` · `PATANJALI, IN OPEN HANDS.`

segments.voice: On the battlefield in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna has just described the yogi whose mind is steady, the same toward friend and enemy. And Arjuna, the finest archer of his age, pushes back. Krishna, he says, the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and stubborn. Holding it seems as hard as holding the wind. Krishna doesn't argue. Yes, he says, the mind is restless and hard to hold. But it can be held, by practice, and by letting go.
screen: `THE STEADY YOGI.` → `AS HARD TO HOLD AS THE WIND.` → `PRACTICE, AND LETTING GO.`

segments.voice: Patanjali names the same pair in the Yoga Sutra: the mind's movements are stilled by abhyasa, practice, and vairagya, letting go. And the first commentary on the Sutra is credited by tradition to Vyasa, the name tradition also gives the sage behind the Mahabharata. In his very first comment, he does something Arjuna would appreciate. He describes the wind. Yoga, he says, is samadhi, the settled, absorbed mind, and the mind has five grounds. Kshipta, scattered, thrown in every direction. Mudha, dull, heavy and fogged over. Vikshipta, distracted, settling now and then but pulled away again. Ekagra, one-pointed, resting on a single thing. And niruddha, stilled, the turnings quieted. Vyasa is strict: the steady moments of a distracted mind don't count as yoga yet, because the distraction swallows them. Yoga proper belongs to the one-pointed and the stilled. But read the list as a weather report, not a grade. It describes skies, not kinds of people, and one person can pass under several before lunch. That's the teaching to carry. Hindu yoga doesn't scold the restless mind; even Arjuna had one. It asks which ground you're on, then hands you the Gita's two tools: come back, again and again, and loosen your grip on what pulls you away.
screen: `ABHYASA AND VAIRAGYA.` · `VYASA: FIVE GROUNDS OF THE MIND.` · `YOGA PROPER: ONE-POINTED, STILLED.` · `A WEATHER REPORT, NOT A GRADE.`

segments.voice: First, just check: is the mind racing, heavy, or coming and going? Name it once, without arguing. Then rest on one thing, the feel of your hands in your lap. When attention drifts, that's the wind; notice it, let go of whatever pulled you, and come back. That coming back is abhyasa. If you pray, you can rest on a name you pray with instead.
Yoga. In Vyasa's first comment, yoga is samadhi, and the mind has five grounds: scattered, dull, distracted, one-pointed and stilled.

1183.title: Ratnakara asks his family
1183.hook: a robber asks his family to share his sin, and Patanjali's sutra on turning a harmful thought around
1183.carry: see where harm ends, then cultivate its opposite
1183.tomorrow: Who is Ishvara in the Yoga Sutra?
1183.howItsDone: In the Yoga Sutras, the counsel to cultivate the opposite sits right after the restraints, such as non-harm, and the observances; students of Yoga philosophy practice it in reflection and in the moment a harmful thought arises, and the robber who became Valmiki is a story Hindu families tell children about owning what you do.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in Yoga: abhyasa and vairagya, practice and letting go, hold a mind as restless as the wind.
screen: `PRACTICE AND LETTING GO.` · `AS HARD TO HOLD AS THE WIND.`

segments.voice: Before he was the poet of the Ramayana, a well-loved later story says, Valmiki was a highway robber named Ratnakara. He stopped travelers in the forest and took what they had, to feed his family. One day he stops a sage, Narada in many tellings, who isn't afraid. The sage asks one question. Your family eats from this. Will they share the sin of it too? Go and ask. Ratnakara goes home and asks. Every one of them says no. The food is ours. The deed is yours.
screen: `A ROBBER IN THE FOREST.` → `WILL THEY SHARE THE SIN?` → `THE DEED IS YOURS.`

segments.voice: Ratnakara follows his harm to where it ends, and it ends with him alone. So he turns. He sits chanting Rama's name so long, the story goes, that an anthill rises over him, valmika, and he comes out as Valmiki. Patanjali puts that same turn into a sutra. Just after the restraints, beginning with ahimsa, non-harm, and the observances, he says, in paraphrase: when thoughts that pull against these trouble you, cultivate the opposite. Pratipaksha bhavana. The next sutra takes the harmful thought apart. It may be done by you, done through someone else, or just approved of. It may come from greed, anger or confusion. It may be mild, middling or intense. Whichever it is, it ends in endless pain and not knowing. Seeing that, cultivate the opposite. So this isn't, think happy thoughts. You follow the thought honestly to where it leads, the way Ratnakara walked home and asked. Many teachers read the story that way. Vyasa's commentary pictures someone tempted to harm remembering why they took up yoga at all. That's the week: a seed, a dancer, a prince, a serpent, a wind. Now a storm, and Yoga's answer. Not fight it, not obey it. Turn it around.
screen: `RATNAKARA BECOMES VALMIKI.` · `CULTIVATE THE OPPOSITE.` · `GREED, ANGER, CONFUSION.` · `FOLLOW IT TO WHERE IT ENDS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small, recent irritation, nothing raw, and let the sharp thought arrive. Without scolding it, follow it a few steps ahead, if I said it, then what, and notice the cost; then let its other side come up, patience, fairness or simple quiet, and rest there for a few breaths. If you pray, you can hold the person you were annoyed with in prayer.
Yoga. In Patanjali's sutras, when a thought against non-harm arrives, yoga means seeing where it ends and cultivating its opposite, pratipaksha bhavana.
screen: `YOGA — today's word`.
